name: Fucoxanthin

card.summary: A brown-seaweed carotenoid sold as a stimulant-free fat-loss supplement, based on rodent UCP1 findings and a few small human trials.
card.aka: Brown seaweed extract, wakame carotenoid, Undaria extract
card.note: Anti-obesity findings come mainly from rodents; Wikipedia notes limited human studies indicate low bioavailability.

quick.overview:
Fucoxanthin is the brown pigment of seaweed and diatoms. It is sold as a fat-loss supplement after a 2005 rodent study linked seaweed lipids with less abdominal fat and more UCP1 expression.

Human research is limited to a few small trials in metabolic syndrome, fatty liver and weight management, several using a microalgae extract.
quick.how: It is taken orally as a seaweed or microalgae extract, typically during a cutting phase and sometimes alongside caffeine or other thermogenics.
quick.risks: Rodents showed no mortality or genotoxicity at high doses, according to Grokipedia, and the pure compound carries a serious-eye-irritation hazard statement. Human safety data are limited.

lead: Fucoxanthin is an orange-brown xanthophyll carotenoid (C42H58O6) that acts as a light-harvesting accessory pigment in brown seaweeds, diatoms and most other heterokont algae, giving them their olive-brown colour. It was first isolated in 1914 by Willstatter and Page from Fucus, Dictyota and Laminaria.[1][2]

People take it as a fat-loss supplement, usually as a brown-seaweed extract (wakame or kombu) or a microalgae extract from diatoms such as Phaeodactylum tricornutum, with the aim of losing abdominal fat, getting leaner and showing more muscle definition. The idea traces to a 2005 rodent study reporting less abdominal white fat and increased UCP1 expression after feeding lipids from the edible seaweed Undaria pinnatifida.[3] Lifters on forums such as T Nation describe it as a 'stimulant-free' thermogenic for cutting phases.[20][21][22]

Reviews describe antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, antidiabetic and anticancer activity, mostly in cells and animals.[4][5] Human research consists of a small number of trials: a 12-week trial in people with metabolic syndrome reported lower body weight and waist circumference in the fucoxanthin group, while a 12-week trial in overweight women on a diet and exercise programme reported no additional weight or fat loss with a fucoxanthin-containing microalgae extract.[12][15][29] A pharmacokinetic study in 18 volunteers followed the main metabolite, fucoxanthinol, in plasma for 24 hours after a kombu extract, and Wikipedia notes that limited human studies indicate low bioavailability.[1][14][29]

paras: Fucoxanthin belongs to the xanthophylls, the oxygen-containing carotenoids. In nature it is bound to protein together with chlorophyll in algal chloroplasts and passes captured light energy to chlorophyll a; Wikipedia states that it accounts for more than 10 percent of estimated natural carotenoid production and, in diatoms such as Phaeodactylum tricornutum, for up to about 60 percent of the energy transfer to chlorophyll a.[1] Seaweeds such as wakame and kombu are staple foods in East and Southeast Asia, so the pigment has a long history of dietary intake, and supplements concentrate it from seaweed or from cultured microalgae.[1][2]

The appearance rationale is a chain: fucoxanthin (or its metabolites) is proposed to raise energy expenditure in fat tissue, reduce abdominal fat accumulation, and so contribute to a leaner midsection and more visible muscle. Rodent data are the origin of that chain; human trials have measured weight, waist circumference, liver and metabolic markers rather than physique photos or body-fat scans.[3][12][15][29]

Grokipedia reports that fucoxanthin was first isolated in 1914 from brown algae, including Fucus, Dictyota and Laminaria species, by Richard Willstatter and H. J. Page, and that its full structure including stereochemistry was worked out with spectroscopic methods in the 1970s.[2] Wikipedia describes it as the pigment that gives brown seaweeds and diatoms their colour and as an accessory light-harvesting pigment in photosynthesis, accounting for more than 10 percent of estimated natural carotenoid production according to Grokipedia.[1][2] Its path into the supplement market followed from the 2005 rodent findings on Undaria lipids and UCP1, which put the molecule into popular discussion as a possible fat-metabolism aid.[3]

Seaweeds such as wakame (Undaria pinnatifida) and kombu (Laminaria japonica) have long been part of traditional diets in East and Southeast Asia, and Grokipedia describes the commercial fucoxanthin market as valued at over 200 million US dollars as of 2024.[2] Reviews of algal carotenoids note that diatoms such as Phaeodactylum tricornutum can hold more fucoxanthin than seaweeds, which is why photobioreactor culture has become an industrial source.[5][6]

Fucoxanthin contains an allenic bond, an epoxide, hydroxyl groups and a conjugated carbonyl group in its polyene chain. It absorbs blue-green to yellow-green light with a peak at about 510 to 525 nm, with a wider range when bound to protein.[1] Wikipedia lists the pure compound under GHS hazard statement H319 (serious eye irritation).[1]

Diatoms are the favoured industrial source because they can hold up to about four times more fucoxanthin than seaweed and can be grown in controlled photobioreactors.[1][6] The molecule is fat-soluble, and Grokipedia reports that it degrades with light, heat and oxygen and that absorption is described as better when consumed with dietary fat.[2] Some products combine it with fucoidan, another brown-seaweed compound.[13]

A 2011 review in Marine Drugs describes how dietary fucoxanthin is converted in the body to metabolites such as fucoxanthinol, and surveys antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, anticancer, anti-obesity and antidiabetic actions seen in laboratory models.[4] Cell studies report radical-scavenging and singlet-oxygen quenching activity for fucoxanthin and its metabolites, and suppression of NF-kB and MAPK inflammatory signalling in lipopolysaccharide-stimulated macrophages.[7][8]

The fat-loss mechanism comes from the 2005 study: UCP1 is a mitochondrial protein that normally dissipates energy as heat in brown adipose tissue, and because adult humans have little brown fat, the authors reasoned that inducing UCP1 in white fat might reduce abdominal fat. Feeding Undaria lipids to rats and mice lowered abdominal white fat weight and produced UCP1 protein signals in white fat.[3] Forum users restate this as fucoxanthin acting as an 'uncoupler'.[21]

A human pharmacokinetic study of kombu extract found plasma fucoxanthinol peaking at about 44 nmol/L around 4 hours after intake in 18 volunteers, with a terminal half-life of about 7 hours; the liver metabolite amarouciaxanthin A was not detected, and the authors concluded that metabolism differs between humans and mice.[14][29]

sections.h: Use in physique and fat-loss communities
paras: On T Nation, fucoxanthin appears in cutting discussions. One member describes it as an uncoupler that works by raising UCP1 and reports better results after adding it, and others recommend it as a stimulant-free thermogenic or as a seaweed-based alternative to a commercial fat-burner that could not be on a banned list.[20][21][22] Posters list it with ephedrine, caffeine, vitamin C and fish oil during a fast, or hope that a new supplement formula would include it among uncouplers.[23][24] Another thread names it as a way to upregulate UCP1 in a discussion about leucine.[25]

Marketing for fucoxanthin products typically emphasises weight management and metabolic support, often as seaweed or microalgae extracts and sometimes as one ingredient in multi-ingredient fat-burner formulas. Reviews of obesity supplements and fat burners mention fucoxanthin among many ingredients, with the underlying human data described as limited.[18][19] On T Nation the compound appears in 2009 to 2010 threads about stimulant-free thermogenics and substitutes for a commercial fat burner, usually as one name on a list rather than as the focus.[20][22][24]
Human research is limited to a few small trials, several of which use mixed products or measure metabolic rather than cosmetic outcomes.[18][19]

Metabolic syndrome (2023). In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2 trial (NCT03613740) in 28 people with metabolic syndrome, a 12-week course of fucoxanthin was followed by a lower body weight (about 80.6 to 79.2 kg), BMI (31.1 to 30.3) and waist circumference (101.2 to 98.9 cm) in the treated group, along with lower blood pressure and higher first-phase and total insulin secretion.[9][12][29]

Overweight women (2024). A 12-week randomized, double-blind trial in 37 overweight women (NCT04761406) gave a Phaeodactylum tricornutum extract standardised for fucoxanthin, or placebo, on top of exercise and a diet reducing intake by about 300 kcal per day. The abstract states that the extract did not promote additional weight loss or fat loss, and it reports preserved bone mass, greater gains in daily steps and aerobic capacity, and improvements in blood lipids, diet adherence and quality of life.[11][15][29]

Fatty liver (2021). A 24-week trial in 42 people with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease tested a combined fucoidan and fucoxanthin product against placebo and reported reductions in liver enzymes, cholesterol, triglycerides, fasting glucose, HbA1c and liver fibrosis scores, with changes in leptin and adiponectin; because two ingredients were combined, effects cannot be attributed to fucoxanthin alone.[13][29] A fucoxanthin-rich supplement for liver health was also registered (NCT03625284, 30 participants).[10]

Absorption and whole-algae trials. Beyond the kombu pharmacokinetic study, a randomized crossover trial in 22 healthy young adults compared two weeks of whole Phaeodactylum biomass with a fish-oil comparator and measured blood omega-3 fatty acids and carotenoids, and a 2022 pilot trial gave the microalgae to 19 healthy older adults for two weeks.[14][16][26] Wikipedia reports that limited human studies indicate low bioavailability, and Grokipedia states that only one obesity-focused trial was reported between 2017 and 2022.[1][2]

Other registered work includes a fucoidan, fucoxanthin and L-carnitine combination in diabetic kidney disease and a microalgae extract tested on cognition and gaming performance, neither of which concerns appearance.[27][28]

A review of fucoxanthin's metabolism, safety and bioactivities describes it as well tolerated in animal studies, and Grokipedia reports no mortality or genotoxicity in rodents at high doses alongside long dietary use of seaweed.[2][4] Human safety data for concentrated supplements are limited to the short trials above. The pure chemical carries the H319 eye-irritation hazard statement.[1] As with other dietary supplements, products are sold as supplement ingredients and the quantity and standardisation of fucoxanthin differ between brands.[18]
A cell study reported that fucoxanthin rescued dexamethasone-induced atrophy in C2C12 myotubes.[17] Laboratory work also examines its antibacterial, anti-inflammatory and anticancer properties.[4][8]

Fucoxanthin sits alongside other non-stimulant fat-loss supplements and seaweed-derived products such as fucoidan, and is discussed with thermogenic ingredients such as caffeine and ephedrine in cutting threads.[19][20][23] General reviews group such ingredients under 'fat burners' and anti-obesity dietary supplements.[18][19]

lore.intro: On T Nation, fucoxanthin is discussed as a stimulant-free fat-loss supplement and 'uncoupler' for cutting phases, usually as one item among several supplements.[20][21][22]

claims.claim: Fucoxanthin raises UCP1 and works as an uncoupler for cutting
claims.believers: Posters say it 'works by increasing levels of UCP1' and report better results and 'good reviews' after adding it.[21][20]
claims.experts: The UCP1 finding comes from a 2005 study in rats and mice; a human kombu study found fucoxanthinol metabolism differs between humans and mice, and Wikipedia notes low bioavailability.[1][3][14]

claims.claim: It is a legal, stimulant-free alternative to banned or stimulant-based fat burners
claims.believers: A poster suggests it is sea-kelp derived, so it should not be on a banned list.[22]
claims.experts: Reviews of fat-loss supplements place fucoxanthin among many products with limited clinical data.[18][19]

claims.claim: It can be stacked with stimulants or other thermogenics for added effect
claims.believers: Members list it with ephedrine, caffeine or usnic acid in cutting stacks.[20][23]
claims.experts: No published trial has tested these combinations.[2]

claims.believers: Forum users expect a leaner midsection from UCP1 induction, echoing the 2005 rodent framing of reduced abdominal fat.[3][20]
claims.experts: A 12-week metabolic-syndrome trial reported small reductions in waist circumference, while a 12-week trial with diet and exercise in overweight women reported no additional fat loss.[12][15][29]

claims.claim: It improves insulin sensitivity and metabolic health, supporting a leaner physique
claims.believers: Supplement marketing and forum posts present it as a metabolic-support ingredient.[22][24]
claims.experts: The metabolic-syndrome trial reported higher insulin secretion and lower blood pressure in the treated group, in 28 participants over 12 weeks; reviews call for larger studies.[12][18][29]

claims.claim: Because it comes from edible seaweed it is safe at supplement intakes
claims.believers: Proponents point to the long history of eating wakame and kombu.[2]
claims.experts: Animal studies report good tolerance and Wikipedia lists only an eye-irritation hazard statement for the pure compound, but human safety data for concentrated supplements come from short trials.[1][2][4]

angle.text: People use fucoxanthin during cutting phases to support fat loss and a leaner look. The mechanism proposed in rodent studies is UCP1 expression in white fat, and trials in people have measured weight, waist and metabolic markers with differing results.[3][12][15][29]
